newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aust. landslide survivor frost-bitten but cheerful.
newsitem.headline: Aust. landslide survivor frost-bitten but cheerful.

text.p: Rescuers on Saturday miraculously plucked a survivor from a concrete tomb beneath the rubble of a three-day-old landslide at an Australian ski village.

Remarkably, ski instructor Stuart Diver escaped serious injury and was said to be in high spirits after his dramatic rescue from deep within the wreckage of two ski lodges engulfed in Wednesday night's landslide at Thredbo village.

But as Diver, 27, was treated for frostbite at a hospital in nearby Canberra late on Saturday night, rescuers unearthed a seventh body from the mangled heap of concrete, twisted metal, dirt and splintered trees at Thredbo, southwest of Sydney.
Police would not name the dead. Still missing in the debris is Diver's wife, Sally.

"He (Diver) is lucid and he is in good spirits and he was even joking with some of the rescue workers," helicopter co-pilot Paul Newland told reporters in Canberra after flying the survivor to the nearest big hospital.
Canberra Hospital's emergency specialist, Dr Bob Dunn, said Diver might need surgery for frostbite.

Diver, described by friends and police as a survival expert and fitness fanatic, spent about 64 hours sandwiched between thick slabs of concrete in a cramped air pocket 10 metres (35 ft) beneath the surface for three freezing nights.
"Stuart's actually in a very good condition," Dunn told reporters in Canberra. "He has some frostbite to his feet, he's otherwise in very good spirits."
Diver is expected to remain in hospital for at least a few days for "extensive treatment", Dunn said.
Diver was found after a fireman heard a muffled voice but rescuers, digging by hand so as not to dislodge the concrete slabs, took 12 hours to free him.
"A miracle has occurred ...", police chief superintendent Charlie Sanderson said after Diver's calls were heard under the tonnes of rubble just before dawn on Saturday.
There was no sign of Diver's wife Sally who was with him in bed on Wednesday night when the slide tore through the resort, sending one lodge crashing into another below it.
More than 150 friends and onlookers gathered around the mountainside cheered as Diver was lifted out of a small hole in the rubble just before sunset.
Diver was placed on a stretcher and quickly covered with several blankets, including a silver thermal blanket, before being carried up a steep slope to a waiting ambulance.
He was later flown by helicopter to a hospital in Canberra, about 150 km (90 miles) north of Thredbo while bells rang out from the village's little chapel.
Borne on a stretcher and wearing a heavy neck-brace, Diver won more cheers on arrival in Canberra, where a crowd of about 60 people shouted their best wishes and tooted car horns.

Meanwhile, rescuers working under floodlights continued to scour the still shifting Thredbo hillside for more survivors. But their only reward was a seventh body, found after Diver's rescue. Heat-seeking probes are being used in the search.

Diver was sandwiched between concrete slabs, which had saved him from being crushed and created an air pocket which insulated him from the freezing overnight temperatures of minus 12 degrees Celsius (about 10 degrees Fahrenheit).
Just before dawn on Saturday fireman Steve Hirst, who was clearing concrete while suspended by a rope, heard a muffled noise and called for silence on the mountain.
"I yelled out: 'rescue team working overhead, can anyone hear me'," Hirst said. "I repeated the call and had a voice come strongly back to me."
"A gentleman identified himself and said he was in fine spirits and doing quite well and uninjured, just extremely cold," he said. Diver's first words were: "I can hear you."
Diver was trapped in a "mini-tomb" created by two concrete slabs, lying on his back, with only 30 cm (12 inches) to move his head and 40 to 50 cm (15 to 19 inches) to move his feet.
There was a cold stream of water running down his side.
Rescuers managed to feed Diver a liquid nutrient solution and warm air was pumped under his jumper to help raise his body temperature, as rescuers continued digging to free him.
Fire Brigade spokesman Ian Krimmer said the area where Diver was found is believed to be a bedroom.
"We are in an area now where there is a chance of other survivors," Krimmer said.
Acting Prime Minister Peter Costello said on Saturday he was thrilled to learn of Diver's survival. "All Australians' hopes and prayers are for his recovery," he said in a statement.
